stoppedItems: ok: none has come back. (1) Larry does not sing or hum anywhere, no band member remarks on a note, there is no music at the table and nobody finishes the busker's tune: `busker-tune` and `busker-behind` stay on the street, unresolved. (2) No tag in which Larry measures himself against a maker: `good-one` thanks the busker, `started-anyway` and `never-ends` are about him only. (3) He never names his job to excuse having no answer: `no-joke` with `i-looked`, and `dont-know`, say he has none and stop there. (4) The sung syllable is 'la' and both sung beats are uncaptioned. (5) Nothing is sung after the street: the last sung beat is four wordless notes behind us at `tune-again`, about two minutes before the close, with no words and nobody addressed.
lookedAtAndPassed: Read against both aired records, lore, the register and every aired line (a word search of the aired scripts for this script's key words finds nothing said before). Looked at hard and passed, nearest first. (a) The welcome, cues `they-look` and `chair-in` with `chair`: every head turns to the one who is outside and holds in silence, a band member accepts them in one flat line, a place is made, the room comes back warmer, a short light exchange, the goodnight. Last week's song took the host in by those same five steps (every head in the band turned to the desk in silence, 'We can work with that.', the key changed to his note, every bulb on, a button, the goodnight), and the pilot's song did it before that. I judge it a different mechanism and not the device that has aired twice: no music stops, no light goes down or comes up, nobody sings, nothing inadequate is offered and made good, no line returns with a word changed, and the one taken in is the viewer, by a rule of hospitality the script has set up at the door. That we end at the table among them is the owner's outline. It is still the third close of three whose feeling is being taken in, and the owner should know (see forTheOwner). (b) `started-without-me` answered by `late`: Larry, apart, expects to be left out, a flat line says otherwise, his chair has been kept. That is the host left out and then taken in, which is how both earlier closes felt about him. The record calls the host left out or small the character and its lines done; this line is new, it is a prediction he gets wrong and not a joke that he is only a host, and no song stops for him. Passed, and put to the owner. (c) The viewer as a camera Larry invites along one unbroken journey with no audience sound (`walk-with-me`, `come-up`): last week's making-of was one continuous shot in which he ushered his own camera in with a run of polite lines, the first of them an invitation to come in, and it ended on a sincere turn to the viewer. There the joke was his manners about an absurd intrusion; here there is no joke, the camera is a person, and the walk and the invitation are the owner's outline. 'Come on up.' is what anyone says at a street door and would not be heard as the earlier line. (d) Saying an unheard person's question aloud as the set-up for an answer (`q-does-it-help`, `q-put-right`, `q-come-up`): last week's interview had the host voice unnamed members' real questions before a guest's real answers. Different job (a conversation, answered by himself), and it is the owner's device. (e) A tune that stops short of its home note (cue `tune-stops`, `never-ends`): last week's ending turned on a chord that wanted one more note. There the gap was filled, wrongly, by the host and made right by the band; here nobody fills it and that is the point. (f) `scarf-on`: the pilot's host had his costume draw itself on at the top as a gag about being newly built, and the show's maker named it a favourite. Here it is the owner's stage direction done without hands, in silence, with no joke on it, and the script's comment already offers the cut to the collar, which avoids the echo; a staging choice. (g) Gold: the scarf and the chair mark what is his by the cast chapter's rule and carry no punch, where last week gold carried two. (h) `no-joke`, `i-looked`, `zhuangzi-name`, `dont-know`, `guest-in-sentence`: the newcomer who is never the expert, not the joke that he is only a host. (i) The wordless holds (`watch-the-cook` 2.4 s, `still-red` 2.6 s, `cross` 5 s): last week's experiment was a stretch of ten seconds or more in which a made thing delivered the turn with the house watching from the edges; here the cook's turn lands on a spoken word and the holds are a head watching, a sign not changing and weather. (j) The dark studio with one pool of light: both aired songs dimmed to a spot on the host for the sincere beat and brought the lights up. Here nothing comes up; the lamp clicks off and we leave. (k) The city in the studio window and the far skyline of the street are light and distance, not the skyline as a gag; staging should keep it so. (l) Sibyl's rule, Eppy calling a ruling, Al's one word, Hy a step ahead, and Pete speaking alone for the first time on air are natures with new content. (m) `always-stop`, `this-block` ('usually') and `never-ends` ('never does') give Larry habits of his own walk home; none points at the show's past. (n) Nobody raises a glass. (o) The goodnight is the owner's line and is not judged.
reason: Nothing in its lines, devices, images, sounds, opening or close does a job an aired episode did in the way that episode did it. It opens on a switched-off studio with no announcer and no title said (the pilot opened on black and built its host; 002-2026-w47 opened on a pen plotter writing the title and the announcer naming the host, which the record warns is one airing short of a ritual). It closes on the owner's lines from a chair at a table, a nod, a hold and a fade, with no song before it, no applause and no toast (the pilot: a key press and a collapsing picture; 002: a toast gesture and the widest shot under long applause). The five stopped items are gone in every form. The two places where it comes nearest the record are the welcome at the table and Larry being wrong about having been left out; both are set out under lookedAtAndPassed with why I pass them, and both go to the owner. No item is turned.
retell: The one where there's no show, so Larry walks you home through the cold, tells you at a red light on an empty road that we don't have to finish it and don't get to quit, and at his own door an old couplet about guests means he cannot leave you on the pavement.
evidence: MOVES 5. The feeling is made by things that happen and no line asks for it. He asks and we answer in a silence nobody hears (`how-have-you-been`, 2.2 s, `yeah-me-too`). `no-joke`, `i-looked`. The hard question is ours, held for 1.6 s before he says it back (cue `listen-put-right`, `q-put-right`), and his first answer is `dont-know`. The quotation gets 1.6 s of silence and then `used-book`. The sign stays red after he has said his piece (cue `still-red`), which is the script declining its own swell. `this-block` said straight ahead, then cue `glance`. We are left on the pavement (cue `listen-door`), `q-come-up`, `position`, the door opened from upstairs (cue `let-in`), `late`, `company`, cue `they-look`, `chair`, cue `chair-in`, and the best direction in it: at `the-meal` nobody is looking at us any more. Every reason I marked the drafts down for on this question has been answered. What is left is pacing at the kerb (see sendBack). INTERESTING 4. One retellable arc, outside to inside, planted as a picture at the restaurant and paid at his door, and held together by three small words that return: 'anyway' (`no-cars`, `started-anyway`), 'started' (`started-anyway`, `started-without-me`, `late`) and 'guest' (`guest-in-sentence`, `guest-2`, `rule`). A viewer would quote `dont-finish` with `dont-quit`, `used-book`, `position` and `chair`. Down a point: until the last block it is still stops on a walk, the busker's point has to be told (`never-ends`) because a wordless phrase in this voice cannot carry it, and the cut test finds `ruling-stands`. TELEVISION 5. A picture meets the words in every scene: the cook stopping on 'slows down' (cue `cook-slows` at -0.5) and then 2.4 s with nothing said; the red of the sign on him from `listen-put-right` to `still-red`; five seconds of snow; the restaurant window again, smaller, over his door (cue `apartment-door`); the camera taking a chair; the bowl going past Larry to our plate (cue `served`). The only words on screen are OPEN, DON'T WALK and WALK, nobody has hands, and every shot from `chair-in` on holds four heads or fewer. The risks are staging's and are listed for the owner: about 54 s at one kerb; three things a viewer must catch that are small on a phone or carried by a head turn (the cook, the watcher in the top window, each `listen-` hold); three single shots of 12 to 17 s under talk (`eyes-front`, `larry-at-glass`, `looks-up`). LARRY 5. The outline's man: slower to joke, about six light lines in four minutes and each one his (`mail-it`, `i-looked`, `zhuangzi-name`, `no-cars`, `position`, `my-house`); personal (`mail-it`, `always-stop`, `used-book`, `this-block`, `started-without-me`); never the expert (`zhuangzi-name`, 'The way I remember it' in `cook-prince`, `dont-know`, `guest-in-sentence`, 'As I remember it' in `guest-1`); able to be wrong (`started-without-me`). The device sounds like talk and no two uses are alike: a question he asks us, three said back after a hold, one look answered without words (cue `our-look`). The crew are themselves and talk to him, not about themselves: `late`, `counted-in`, `long-way`, `chair`, `still-the-rule`. IDEAS 4. Three things a person could do, from three cultures, arriving three ways: seen and then told (the cook), asked for after he admits he has no answer (Tarfon), and done instead of told (the couplet, which the table then does back to him at `rule`). All in the cards' safe wordings as far as I can see; the quotation matches its card to the word. Down a point: the plain form of the central idea (`dont-finish`, `dont-quit`) arrives about seventeen seconds after a sentence in the English of 1913 that few will parse on one hearing in this voice; with the summing-up line gone, that the cook's story is meant for us rests wholly on a silhouette going slowly while a room hurries; and the third idea opens on the same sentence as the first (`cook-story`, `tamil-book`), with the hardest name in the script, at the moment it is meant to be an act. I have not heard it: every score on sound rests on the script and its cues.
fixedPoints: ok. The five owner's lines are in their places and nothing reads as a joke on them: `no-show` and `paycheck` open it, `walk-with-me` is the ask, the table line is two consecutive beats (`mixed-up-world`, `keep-close`) with no cue and no sound beat between them, and `stay-warm` is the last beat with nothing after it. The viewer makes footsteps and nothing else. Each say-back has its own `listen-` cue and a held gap of 1.2 to 1.6 s. The holiday and the dish are unnamed. No laugh, applause or sting: the only effects are `whoosh`, `tick` and `murmur`, and Dee's laugh is a voiced line. On screen: OPEN, DON'T WALK, WALK, a blank envelope. We are seated, served and still at the table on the last picture. 408 words by the brief's count (397 spoken, 11 sung). Two things the owner should see, neither a break: `mail-it` sits directly after the paycheck line and makes it a pretext, in Larry's own mouth and as a confession; and the owner's comma in the table line has become a full stop and a 0.7 s breath.

reasons.reason: The first idea is the one a viewer would miss least
reasons.note: Gone whole. The first idea is now the cook, and it starts from something he has stopped to look at (`always-stop`, `one-cook`).

reasons.reason: The three ideas have one shape
reasons.note: The cook is seen, told and left in silence; Tarfon is asked for, quoted, placed and borrowed while the street does nothing; the couplet is his reason for an act. What survives of the old shape is one sentence frame used twice (`cook-story`, `tamil-book`).
Cut; 2.4 s of the cook going slowly at `watch-the-cook`. The cost is that nothing now says the story is for us; the picture has to.

The sign stays red for 2.6 s after `dont-quit` and changes on one tick with no chirp, look or remark. Whether 2.6 s reads as the sign's own time, and not as a late answer or as nothing happening, is staging's to prove.

reasons.reason: The table is a welcome party, not a meal
reasons.note: They waited, a place is made in front of us, we are served, bowls go both ways, and Pete, Hy and Dee each have something to do. But the meal running with nobody speaking to us or about us is 3.2 s (cue `the-meal`) before he turns to camera; the rest of it is behind his three lines and in the last hold. About 23 of the table's 40 seconds are still arrival: three lines on lateness, a ruling, its appeal and its call.

reasons.reason: `house-rule` states the welcome as a principle
reasons.note: Cut. The welcome is one word and a chair; Sibyl's rule is procedure and costs Larry something.

It is now the event of the piece: outside the glass at the restaurant, outside it again at `apartment-door`, left on the pavement at `listen-door`, `q-come-up`, the couplet, `position`, the door from upstairs.

reasons.reason: Would not be missed: `full-house`, the steam grate, `house-record`
reasons.note: All three are gone. `dee-laughs` is kept and now has a cause.

joins: `used-book` (one draft), `guest-in-sentence` (another) and `borrow` (the base) all sit between the quotation and its plain reading. `guest-in-sentence` and `borrow` each say the sentence is not his, back to back, in two different figures (a guest, then a borrower). From the end of `tarfon-2` to `dont-finish` is about seventeen seconds where the base took about eight. It is the one place where the script reads as having taken something from everybody.

`cook-story` and `tamil-book` come from two drafts and open on the same frame ('There's ... an old Chinese book' / 'There's an old Tamil book ...'). By the second, a viewer hears another book arriving before they hear his reason for not going up.

`late`, `counted-in`, `long-way`: three lines in a row that say he is late, from two drafts. They go quickly (about six seconds) and `long-way` hands him `company`, so the join holds, but it is the pile-up the select notes marked down as a second beat on lateness.

`my-house` was written to answer a rule that had the word 'house' in it. It now answers 'the guest is served first', and reads only if the bowl is seen to go past him (cue `served`). It rests on staging.

`what-helped` says people were rattled then, 'too'. The line that first said 'rattled' went out with the old first question, so the word now arrives with nothing before it but our unheard answer and `yeah-me-too`. It holds, and is arguably better: the silence gets its name fifteen seconds late.

`this-block` and the cue `glance` were the set-up for a line that was cut. They now pay off at `company`. The join holds; what went with the cut is the one place where he said, in someone else's words, that he was glad of us.

No change of voice that I can hear between the three writers' lines. `mail-it` makes `always-stop`, `this-block` and `never-ends` one man's habit, which is what lets lines from three drafts sound like one walk.
wouldNotBeMissed: `ruling-stands`: it announces the result of an exchange that has already ended on its own dry button (`still-the-rule`). It is there so that Eppy speaks and Dee has something to laugh at, and it is the loudest voice in the piece four seconds before the quietest lines.

One of the two acknowledgements at the kerb (the second sentence of `guest-in-sentence`, or the figure in `borrow`): both say the sentence is not his. The better line is the first; the second is the one that marks the reading as his own.

The title in `tamil-book` said aloud at the door: the idea is the couplet, and the name is the hardest word in the script at the moment a viewer is waiting to be let in. (The same could be said of `zhuangzi-name`, except that its second sentence is Larry.)
sendBack: Small. `used-book`, `guest-in-sentence`, `borrow`: about seventeen seconds and twenty-nine words between the end of the quotation and the plain reading a viewer is waiting for, at a kerb, in the longest stand of the walk (about 54 s from `crossing-red` to `walk-sign`). Two of the three lines do the same job.
Small. `tamil-book` opens on the frame `cook-story` used, so the idea that is meant to be an act announces itself as a third book.

Small. Cue `the-meal`: 3.2 s is the whole of the meal that runs before he turns to us. The outline's last picture is a large group of close friends sharing a meal, and most of the table's time still goes on the arrival.
Small. `late`, `counted-in`, `long-way`: three beats on lateness in a row.
forTheOwner: From the record, for you and not for a writer: this is the third close of three whose feeling is someone being taken in. The pilot's song and last week's song each took Larry in; this one takes the viewer in, and it does it with a held silence, every head turned, one flat line from the band and a place made, which is step for step how last week's song took Larry. I passed it as a different mechanism (no music, no lights, no sung note, a rule of hospitality and a chair), and your outline is what puts us at the table. You kept last week's ending on purpose; you should decide this one knowing it.

`started-without-me` ('They'll have started without me.') is the line that makes the table take Larry in as well as us: he expects to be left out and is wrong. Larry left out and then taken in is how both earlier closes felt about him. With the line, `late` corrects him; without it, 'Nobody has started.' is only news to us and the table is about the guest alone. It could go either way; I would rather you chose it than a gate did.
`mail-it` follows your paycheck line and admits the paycheck is a pretext. It is the most personal line in the first minute and both reviewers wanted it; it does change what your line is.

Your table line is one sentence with a comma in the outline; here it is two sentences with a 0.7 s breath between them and nothing else. Your goodnight is a wish and then a goodnight with a word for the audience before it, as last week's close was in other words. Both are yours and neither was judged.

The light. As written it stays red and nobody remarks on it, so from `no-cars` to `position`, about 85 seconds, there is no light line at all. The other way (it changes on his last word and he disowns it) gives the crossing its one laugh and makes the street answer him. I think as written is right for a man who has just said he does not know, but it leaves the middle of the piece without relief by design.

The third idea. The Tamil couplet at the door makes coming in an event and is the only idea Larry does instead of tells. What it replaced, the Norse line on the last block, was the one moment he said he was glad of the company. The last block now says it with a glance, and `company` says it to the table.

The names. 'The Zhuangzi', 'Tarfon' and 'the Tirukkural' are said aloud. The voice will find all three hard and the captions will carry them; `zhuangzi-name` makes that honest in Larry's mouth. The third comes at the door, where it costs most.

Near a limit, and the auditor's to rule: `guest-in-sentence` names Torah and the piece quotes a rabbi, where chapter 9 keeps religion out even as a reference. The special is being made on the reading in special.md that you are asked to confirm. `fast-and-fair` and `q-put-right` are the nearest it comes to 'justice seems rare' and name nothing. The exchange about serving the guest first comes about twenty seconds after the Tamil text; the joke is on Larry and not on the book.

Rests on staging. (1) Each `listen-` hold has to read as us speaking; if it does not, the three say-backs are rhetorical questions. (2) The cook is a silhouette at the back of a window on a phone, and the first idea is in what he does. (3) At `let-in` the door opens because somebody upstairs saw us, and the only sign of that is one small figure in a top-floor window; if it is missed, the door opens by itself on his cue, which is what the crossing was rewritten to avoid. (4) The gold chair has to read as Larry's, kept for him, or the second chair is a puzzle. (5) `scarf-on`: a scarf that draws itself on will remind anyone who saw the pilot of his costume doing the same; the script already allows a cut to the collar instead. (6) Nobody should lift a glass at the table: last week closed on a toast. (7) The stock title and end cards would put a lit studio before the dark one and after the table, under the credits' usual heading; that is with the project manager.

Rests on hearing. The busker must not sound like Al, who speaks at the table two minutes later, and whether the tune can be heard to stop short is doubtful; `never-ends` covers it. The quotation is in the English of 1913. This is the first time Pete speaks alone. Eppy's call is a shout four seconds before your quietest line. 'Rabbi', 'Tarfon' and 'Torah' in this voice want your ears in particular: best effort stands, but not if one of them is heard as something else.

Length. 243 seconds by arithmetic and 408 words, which is the floor of the range: it is long on silence, not on talk. If it has to come down, the writer offers the busker's second phrase and `never-ends`; those are also the only things that tell a viewer the tune is unfinished, which is what rhymes it with the crossing.
